why: An unknown 'Pellbrook Institute' on a domain registered 16 days ago recites her employer, role and tenure from the team page to harvest a member ID and a direct phone number.
A routine running-late note asking her to start a meeting, with no link, payment, credential or data request and nothing drawn from her footprint.
Impersonates her school's alumni office from a lookalike domain registered on 2026-09-16 (the real one dates from 2007) and uses her name variants to steer her into an identity-check phone call.
Names her public booking page to push her to a 3-week-old 'support' domain where she is asked for her scheduling account e-mail and password.
A plain alumni newsletter from the school's long-established domain (2007) with no request beyond an optional unsubscribe.
A CPD deadline reminder from a professional body's 2008 domain that links only to its own member area and asks for nothing sensitive in the message.
A speaking invitation from the institute's established domain; the 3-month-old event-programme site fits a dated forum and nothing sensitive is requested.
A routine membership renewal from the institute's 2008 domain with direct debit as the default, no new payee and no urgency beyond a normal annual deadline.
A 9-day-old domain uses her podcast episode to get her to forward an SMS verification code, which is a classic account-takeover move.
A standard sign-in notice from an identity provider's 2015 domain that asks for no action if the sign-in was hers and gives no link, sending her to her own account settings instead.
A local charity regatta organiser openly says how she found the address and only asks her to present prizes; the young event site fits a new 2027 event and nothing sensitive is requested.
An unknown 'filing agent' on a 5-week-old domain quotes her public director number to harvest the private items it lacks: home address, birth year and phone.
An SMS posing as her firm's IT asks her to reply with her authenticator code, which no real IT team requests and which hands over her account.
A low-stakes address check from the school's long-established domain that needs no reply if the address is right and asks for no credentials or payment.
A 'new number' friend lure uses her location and sailing to send her to a 5-day-old album domain that wants her to 'confirm it's you', a credential or account-takeover step.

A penalty demand with a deadline that escalates the amount and threatens recovery, payable to a third party's link or account and quoting her public director number, is a payment-fraud pattern whatever the domain's age.
The podcast host asks permission to point a listener to her already-public notes page, with no link, payment or data requested.
A reunion notice from the school's established 2007 domain, which itself vouches for the class committee's event site, and nothing sensitive is requested.
A lookalike of her firm's domain (vennho1t, digit 1 for letter l), registered 3 days ago, sends a 'secure share' link posing as a colleague.

A confidential 'witness' notice says it comes from her association, uses a domain she cannot confirm as its own, asks for her director number and phone and tells her to keep it secret, so she should check with the association through a known contact first.
Speaker logistics from the podcast's 2019 domain about an event she has already agreed to, asking only for low-risk items (diet, AV needs, bio, headshot), with an e-mail alternative to the form.
An unknown 'filing agent' on a 4-week-old domain uses her director number and firm to send her to a 2-week-old portal for her password and a photo ID.
An unverifiable WhatsApp headhunter builds the brief from her public profile and asks for her CV before naming the client, so she should verify the firm independently first.
A 'Pellbrook Institute' directory she is not linked to, on a domain registered a month ago, puts together her public details and pressures her to 'confirm' through its own link before a deadline.

A cold headhunter approach built from her public profile, with a personalised link that expires in 72 hours, comes from an aged domain, so she should confirm the firm through a known channel before opening it.
A plausible small club shortfall, but it is a bank-transfer request from an unverified WhatsApp contact, so she should confirm with the club through its known channel before paying.
An 18-day-old 'renewals service' uses her director number and personal site to move her off her firm address and onto its own confirmation link before a fee deadline.
A 2-day-old lookalike of her firm's domain poses as a colleague, asks her to call a personal mobile and keep it from a colleague, which is the CEO-fraud pattern.
